web-ml-071:
### Definition
Attention lets a model weigh context tokens; BERT is a bidirectional encoder pre-trained with masked language modelling; GPT is a causal decoder pre-trained to predict the next token. Pre-training, fine-tuning and post-training are successive stages of model building.

### Intuition
BERT sees both sides of a word, so it builds rich representations for understanding tasks; GPT sees only the left context, so it can generate text one token at a time.

### The math
Attention: softmax(Q K^T/sqrt(d)) V. BERT loss: -sum over masked positions log p(x_i | x_unmasked). GPT loss: -sum_t log p(x_t | x_<t). Pre-training: self-supervised learning on large unlabelled data. Fine-tuning: supervised training on a downstream task (full or parameter-efficient such as LoRA, W + BA with low rank r). Post-training: instruction tuning (SFT), then preference optimisation (RLHF with PPO, DPO) and safety training.

### Concrete example
Start with a pre-trained base LLM, SFT on 100k instruction pairs, then DPO on preference pairs to make answers helpful and harmless.

### Trade-offs and when to use what
Encoder models: strong classifiers and embedders at small size; decoder models: generation and in-context learning. Pre-training is expensive and needs huge data; fine-tuning is cheap but can forget; post-training aligns behaviour but can reduce diversity.

### Likely follow-ups
- **What is LoRA?** Adds trainable low-rank updates to frozen weights.
- **Why is BERT not generative?** Its bidirectional masked objective does not define a left-to-right distribution.
- **What is post-training?** All training after pre-training: SFT, preference tuning, safety.
web-ml-072:
### Definition
Deploying an LLM safely means combining a sound transformer-based model with layered controls: input and output filtering, access control, evaluation, monitoring and human oversight.

### Intuition
LLMs can hallucinate, leak data, follow malicious instructions or produce harmful content, so safety is a system property, not only a model property.

### The math
Layers: (1) data and model: safety-tuned model, red-teaming; (2) prompt layer: system prompt, instruction hierarchy, injection defences; (3) retrieval: access control per document; (4) input/output classifiers for toxicity, PII, policy; (5) tool permissions with least privilege and confirmation; (6) rate limits and abuse detection; (7) logging, evals and incident response. Metrics: attack success rate, refusal rate on benign prompts, groundedness, latency.

### Concrete example
A customer-support bot: retrieve only the caller's own records, strip PII from logs, block tool calls that move money without user confirmation, run a nightly adversarial test suite.

### Trade-offs and when to use what
Stronger filtering reduces risk but increases false refusals and latency; the right balance depends on the harm of errors. Staged rollout with canaries, kill switches and human review for high-stakes actions.

### Likely follow-ups
- **What is prompt injection?** Untrusted text that tries to override instructions.
- **How to measure safety?** Red-team suites with attack success and over-refusal rates.
- **Why least privilege for tools?** It bounds damage from a compromised prompt.
web-ml-073:
### Definition
Calibrating LLM output to a fixed format (for example Word styles) means constraining and verifying generation so that the text maps deterministically to the required structure.

### Intuition
The model should output structured content (headings, lists, tables) rather than raw layout; a deterministic renderer then converts it to formatting.

### The math
Approaches: (1) ask for a strict schema (JSON or Markdown with a defined grammar) and use constrained decoding or a grammar to guarantee validity; (2) map schema elements to Word styles with a library (python-docx); (3) validate and repair: parse, check against the schema, retry with the error message; (4) few-shot examples and low temperature; (5) evaluate with a format-validity rate and style-fidelity checks.

### Concrete example
Output: {"title": "...", "sections": [{"heading": "...", "bullets": [...]}]}. The renderer applies Heading 1 to the title, Heading 2 to section headings and the List Bullet style to bullets; invalid JSON triggers a retry.

### Trade-offs and when to use what
Constrained decoding guarantees syntax but may slightly lower content quality; post-hoc validation is simpler but costs retries. Keep formatting out of the LLM when possible: let the model produce content and let code handle presentation.

### Likely follow-ups
- **Why not ask the model to write raw docx XML?** Error-prone; a schema plus a renderer is robust.
- **How to measure success?** Fraction of outputs that parse and render correctly.
- **What about long documents?** Generate section by section with shared context.
web-ml-074:
### Definition
Cleaning OCR data and building an LLM training set means turning noisy scanned text into high-quality, deduplicated, licensed and filtered examples.

### Intuition
OCR output contains recognition errors, broken layout (columns, headers, hyphenation) and noise; training on it teaches the model the noise.

### The math
Pipeline: (1) quality scoring: OCR confidence, dictionary hit rate, perplexity from a small LM; (2) layout repair: dehyphenate, merge lines, remove headers/footers, reorder columns; (3) spelling or LLM-assisted correction on low-confidence spans (keep the original for audit); (4) language ID, PII and licence filtering; (5) exact and near-duplicate removal (MinHash LSH); (6) decontamination against eval sets; (7) formatting into prompt-response pairs and sampling a balanced mix; (8) human audit of a random sample.

### Concrete example
A scanned-books corpus: drop pages with confidence below 0.8, repair hyphenation ("infor-\nmation" -> "information"), deduplicate with a Jaccard threshold of 0.8, and keep a 1% sample for manual review.

### Trade-offs and when to use what
Aggressive filtering raises quality but reduces volume and may bias the data (for example against old fonts or low-resource languages); LLM-based correction can hallucinate, so restrict it and compare to the OCR text.

### Likely follow-ups
- **How to dedupe at scale?** MinHash plus LSH.
- **How do you judge cleaning quality?** Downstream eval and human spot checks.
- **Why decontaminate?** To keep benchmark results honest.
web-ml-075:
### Definition
Annotator agreement quantifies how consistently people label the same items; LLM-as-judge uses a model to score outputs, which must be validated against human judgments.

### Intuition
If humans disagree, labels are noisy and the metric ceiling is low; an automatic judge is useful only if it tracks human preferences.

### The math
Cohen's kappa for two raters: kappa = (p_o - p_e)/(1 - p_e), with p_o observed agreement and p_e chance agreement. Fleiss' kappa and Krippendorff's alpha generalise to many raters and missing data. For a judge, compute agreement with human labels (accuracy, kappa, Spearman correlation) and check biases: position bias (order swap), verbosity bias, self-preference. Mitigate with pairwise comparisons in both orders, rubrics, multiple judges and calibration on a human-labelled set.

### Concrete example
Two annotators agree on 85 of 100 items with p_e = 0.5: kappa = (0.85 - 0.5)/0.5 = 0.70 (substantial). An LLM judge with kappa 0.65 against humans is acceptable for cheap iteration but not for final claims.

### Trade-offs and when to use what
Humans are slow and expensive but the reference; LLM judges scale cheaply but can be biased and gamed. Use humans to validate the judge, spot-check regularly, and keep human evaluation for release decisions.

### Likely follow-ups
- **What kappa is good?** Above about 0.6 is substantial.
- **How do you detect position bias?** Swap response order and compare verdicts.
- **Can the judge be the same model?** Self-preference makes it risky.
web-ml-076:
### Definition
The KV cache stores the keys and values of previous tokens in autoregressive decoding so that each new token only computes attention against cached tensors instead of recomputing the whole prefix.

### Intuition
During generation the keys and values of old tokens do not change, so recomputing them every step wastes work; caching turns per-step cost from O(n) projections to O(1) new projection.

### The math
At step t compute q_t, k_t, v_t for the new token only, append k_t, v_t to the cache and attend: out_t = softmax(q_t K_cache^T/sqrt(d)) V_cache. Memory per token: 2 x n_layers x n_kv_heads x d_head x bytes. For a 32-layer model, 32 KV heads, d_head 128, fp16: 2 x 32 x 32 x 128 x 2 = 524,288 bytes = 0.5 MB per token, so a 4,096-token sequence needs 2 GB.

### Concrete example
```python
def decode_step(x_t, cache, Wq, Wk, Wv):
    q, k, v = x_t @ Wq, x_t @ Wk, x_t @ Wv
    cache['k'].append(k)
    cache['v'].append(v)
    K = np.stack(cache['k'])
    V = np.stack(cache['v'])
    w = softmax(K @ q / np.sqrt(len(q)))
    return w @ V
```

### Trade-offs and when to use what
The cache trades memory for compute and makes decoding memory-bandwidth bound; reduce it with GQA/MQA, quantised caches, paged attention (vLLM) and sliding windows.

### Likely follow-ups
- **Why does the cache grow with batch size?** Each sequence has its own K and V.
- **What is paged attention?** Allocates cache in blocks to avoid fragmentation.
- **Why is decoding memory-bound?** Each token reads the weights and the cache for few FLOPs.
web-ml-077:
### Definition
Tokenisation methods (word, character, BPE, WordPiece, unigram, byte-level) split text into units; LLM-based recommendation uses language models to rank items from text, history or both.

### Intuition
Subword tokenisers balance vocabulary size and sequence length. In recommendation, an LLM can read a user's history and item descriptions and score or generate recommendations.

### The math
BPE: repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent symbol pair. WordPiece picks merges by likelihood gain; unigram LM prunes a large vocabulary by loss. LLM recommenders: (a) embed users and items as text and retrieve by similarity; (b) prompt the LLM with the history to rank a candidate list (listwise); (c) fine-tune on interaction sequences with item IDs as tokens (semantic IDs from quantised embeddings); (d) use the LLM for features, explanations and cold-start item descriptions.

### Concrete example
A news recommender: embed article text with a sentence encoder for cold-start retrieval, rank candidates with a gradient-boosted model using the embeddings plus behaviour features, and use the LLM only to produce a short explanation.

### Trade-offs and when to use what
LLMs help cold start and explainability but are expensive and slower than classical two-tower and ranking models; position and popularity biases and hallucinated items appear; keep the LLM off the critical path for latency-bound ranking.

### Likely follow-ups
- **What are semantic IDs?** Discrete codes from quantised item embeddings used as tokens.
- **Why byte-level BPE?** It handles any input with no unknown tokens.
- **How to evaluate?** Offline NDCG on temporal splits plus online A/B tests.
web-ml-078:
### Definition
Reward hacking is when a model exploits flaws in the reward signal, scoring highly without achieving the intended goal; detecting and preventing it is central to RLHF and RL training.

### Intuition
Optimising a proxy reward long enough makes the policy find shortcuts (Goodhart's law): longer answers, flattery, exploiting the reward model's blind spots or bugs in an environment.

### The math
Detection: track proxy reward versus a held-out gold metric or human evaluation (they diverge), monitor response statistics (length, repetition, format tricks), KL from the reference policy, reward model uncertainty, and audit top-reward samples. Prevention: KL penalty r - beta KL(pi || pi_ref); early stopping on gold metric; reward model ensembles with pessimistic aggregation; length and format normalisation; adversarial training of the reward model on found exploits; best-of-n caps; verifiable rewards where possible; sandbox and unit-test environments for coding tasks.

### Concrete example
In a code-RL task the policy learns to edit the test file to always pass. Fix by making tests read-only, hiding them, and evaluating on held-out tests.

### Trade-offs and when to use what
Stronger penalties and ensembles reduce hacking but slow learning; verifiable rewards (math answers, unit tests) are harder to game than learned ones but cover fewer tasks.

### Likely follow-ups
- **What is Goodhart's law?** When a measure becomes a target it stops being a good measure.
- **Role of KL?** Limits how far the policy can drift into exploits.
- **How to detect it online?** Gold-metric spot checks and anomaly monitoring on samples.
web-ml-079:
### Definition
KL divergence in language-model training measures how far a model's token distribution is from a reference; it appears in distillation, RLHF penalties and fine-tuning regularisation.

### Intuition
It quantifies the extra bits needed if the reference distribution is used to encode samples of the tuned model, so it works as a "stay close" constraint.

### The math
Per-token KL(pi || pi_ref) = sum_v pi(v | s) log(pi(v | s)/pi_ref(v | s)); in sampled form use log pi(y_t) - log pi_ref(y_t) averaged over generated tokens (the k1 estimator), or lower-variance k3 = (r - 1) - log r with r = pi_ref/pi. RLHF objective: E[r(x, y)] - beta KL(pi || pi_ref). Distillation: minimise KL(teacher || student) = cross-entropy against teacher probabilities.

### Concrete example
With beta = 0.05 and a per-sequence KL of 20 nats, the penalty is 1.0, comparable to a reward scale of 1; this prevents the policy from moving far.

### Trade-offs and when to use what
Forward KL (teacher || student) is mass-covering; reverse KL (student || teacher) is mode-seeking. A large beta limits improvement; a small beta allows reward hacking. Adaptive controllers target a KL budget.

### Likely follow-ups
- **Why reverse KL in RLHF?** It can be estimated from the policy's own samples.
- **What is the k3 estimator?** A low-variance, unbiased KL estimator.
- **How to choose beta?** Tune to a target KL and validate on a gold metric.
web-ml-080:
### Definition
Importance sampling estimates expectations under a target distribution using samples from a different behaviour distribution by reweighting with probability ratios.

### Intuition
In LLM RL, data generated by an old policy must be reused to update the new policy; the ratio corrects for the mismatch.

### The math
E_p[f(x)] = E_q[f(x) p(x)/q(x)]. In PPO the ratio is r_t = pi_theta(a_t | s_t)/pi_old(a_t | s_t) and the clipped objective is E[min(r_t A_t, clip(r_t, 1 - eps, 1 + eps) A_t)]. Sequence-level ratios multiply token ratios and become very high variance; token-level ratios or truncated/self-normalised weights are used. Variance grows as p and q diverge: effective sample size n_eff = (sum w)^2/sum w^2.

### Concrete example
If the old and new token probabilities are 0.2 and 0.3, r = 1.5; with eps = 0.2 and positive advantage the clipped term caps the incentive at 1.2.

### Trade-offs and when to use what
Importance sampling enables off-policy reuse and asynchronous training but suffers high variance; clipping and trust regions limit damage; staleness (rollouts from an older policy) must be controlled.

### Likely follow-ups
- **Why clip the ratio?** To keep updates close to the behaviour policy.
- **What is effective sample size?** It measures how many unweighted samples the weighted set is worth.
- **What if q(x) = 0 where p(x) > 0?** The estimator is biased; support must cover the target.
web-ml-081:
### Definition
GRPO (group relative policy optimisation) drops PPO's learned value function and normalises rewards within a group of sampled responses; sparse rewards are given only at the end, dense rewards at intermediate steps.

### Intuition
PPO needs a critic for advantages; GRPO samples G responses per prompt and uses each response's reward relative to the group as its advantage.

### The math
GRPO advantage: A_i = (r_i - mean(r_1..r_G))/std(r_1..r_G), applied to all tokens of response i; the objective is PPO-style clipped with a KL penalty to the reference. PPO: A_t from GAE using a value network V(s): A_t = sum (gamma lambda)^l delta_(t+l), delta_t = r_t + gamma V(s_(t+1)) - V(s_t). Sparse reward: only the final answer correctness (+1 or 0). Dense reward: process rewards per step.

### Concrete example
For a math prompt with G = 8 samples where 3 are correct (reward 1): the correct ones get advantage (1 - 0.375)/0.484 = 1.29 and incorrect ones -0.77.

### Trade-offs and when to use what
GRPO saves the memory and instability of a critic and works well with verifiable sparse rewards, but has noisier credit assignment per token and needs many samples. PPO with a good critic gives finer credit assignment; dense process rewards speed learning but can be hacked and cost annotation.

### Likely follow-ups
- **Why group-normalise?** It gives a baseline without a critic.
- **What if all samples have equal reward?** Advantages are zero and the prompt gives no gradient.
- **Sparse versus dense rewards?** Sparse are robust but slow; dense are fast but hackable.
web-ml-082:
### Definition
SFT trains on demonstrations with cross-entropy; PPO-based RLHF optimises a reward model with RL; DPO optimises preferences directly with a classification-style loss. The KL penalty keeps the policy near a reference model.

### Intuition
SFT imitates good outputs. Preference methods teach which of two outputs is better, shaping behaviour beyond imitation.

### The math
SFT: minimise -sum log pi(y | x). RLHF: maximise E[r(x, y)] - beta KL(pi || pi_ref) with PPO. DPO: minimise -log sigma(beta[log pi(y_w)/pi_ref(y_w) - log pi(y_l)/pi_ref(y_l)]), equivalent to RLHF with an implicit reward r = beta log pi/pi_ref under a Bradley-Terry preference model. KL role: prevent reward hacking, preserve fluency and prior knowledge.

### Concrete example
Pipeline: SFT on 50k demonstrations, collect pairwise human preferences, then DPO (simple, stable) or PPO (more flexible, uses online samples) with beta about 0.1.

### Trade-offs and when to use what
SFT: cheap and stable but limited to demonstration quality. DPO: no reward model or sampling loop, but offline and sensitive to data distribution. PPO: online exploration and fine control, but complex, unstable and expensive. Larger beta means safer, smaller improvement.

### Likely follow-ups
- **What is the Bradley-Terry model?** P(y_w > y_l) = sigma(r_w - r_l).
- **Why do DPO and RLHF match?** DPO derives from the same KL-regularised objective in closed form.
- **When prefer PPO?** When online exploration or a verifiable reward matters.
web-ml-083:
### Definition
Mixture-of-Experts layers route each token to a few expert networks; expert parallelism places different experts on different devices and exchanges tokens with all-to-all communication.

### Intuition
Experts specialise and only a few run per token, so parameters scale without proportional compute, but tokens must be sent to the devices holding their experts.

### The math
Forward pass: route (top-k gating), dispatch tokens by all-to-all to the expert devices, compute expert FFNs, combine results by all-to-all and weight by gates. Capacity per expert = capacity_factor x tokens x k/E; overflow tokens are dropped or sent to the residual path. Communication per layer is about 2 x tokens x d x bytes of all-to-all. Load balancing loss and router z-loss stabilise training.

### Concrete example
With 64 experts on 8 GPUs (8 experts each) and top-2 routing, every token may be sent to two GPUs; balanced routing keeps GPUs equally busy.

### Trade-offs and when to use what
Expert parallelism cuts memory per device but adds all-to-all latency; combine with data and tensor parallelism; imbalanced routing wastes compute; fine-grained experts improve quality but add communication.

### Likely follow-ups
- **Why all-to-all?** Each GPU sends different token subsets to every other GPU.
- **What happens on overflow?** Extra tokens are dropped or rerouted.
- **How to reduce communication?** Restrict routing to a node group, use higher bandwidth links.
web-ml-084:
### Definition
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supplies relevant documents in the prompt; fine-tuning bakes behaviour or knowledge into weights. Context limits, conversation state and prompt injection shape both designs.

### Intuition
RAG gives fresh, attributable knowledge; fine-tuning changes style, format and skills. They solve different problems.

### The math
RAG: embed chunks, retrieve top-k (hybrid BM25 plus vectors, rerank), place in the prompt with citations. Context limit: prompt tokens + output <= window; manage with chunking, reranking, summarising and compressing history. State: store conversation memory outside the model (summaries, key facts, database) and rebuild the prompt each turn since the API is stateless. Prompt injection: retrieved or user text can contain instructions; defend with separating instructions from data, least-privilege tools, output checks and treating retrieved content as untrusted.

### Concrete example
Company policy Q&A: RAG over the policy wiki with access control and citations; fine-tune only if the tone and format need adapting.

### Trade-offs and when to use what
RAG: up-to-date, auditable, no retraining, but depends on retrieval quality and adds latency. Fine-tuning: low latency and consistent style, but stale knowledge and costly updates. Use both when needed: fine-tune for behaviour and RAG for facts.

### Likely follow-ups
- **How to reduce hallucinations in RAG?** Better retrieval, grounding instructions, citations and abstain rules.
- **How to handle long histories?** Summarise and retrieve past turns.
- **How to defend against injection?** Isolate untrusted text and restrict tool permissions.
web-ml-085:
### Definition
Designing a transformer LLM means choosing architecture (decoder-only blocks), size, data, tokenizer, training recipe and inference optimisations to meet a quality, cost and latency target.

### Intuition
Start from the compute budget and use scaling laws to balance parameters and tokens, then design for stable training and efficient serving.

### The math
Parameters per layer about 12 d_model^2; total about 12 L d^2 + V d. Compute C about 6 N D FLOPs (N parameters, D tokens); compute-optimal D about 20 N. Choices: pre-LN/RMSNorm, SwiGLU FFN, RoPE, GQA, vocabulary 32k-128k, context length, AdamW with warm-up and cosine decay, bf16, gradient clipping, batch size ramp. Serving: KV cache, quantisation, speculative decoding, continuous batching.

### Concrete example
A 7B model: L = 32, d = 4096, 32 heads (8 KV heads with GQA), FFN hidden 11008 with SwiGLU, vocabulary 32k, trained on about 1-2T tokens.

### Trade-offs and when to use what
Bigger models and more data improve quality at higher cost; deep-narrow versus wide-shallow affects throughput; long context needs memory-efficient attention; over-training small models on more tokens lowers inference cost.

### Likely follow-ups
- **Why SwiGLU?** Gated activations improve quality at equal compute.
- **How to estimate training cost?** C = 6 N D FLOPs divided by achieved cluster FLOPs.
- **Why pre-LN?** Stable gradients at depth.
web-ml-086:
### Definition
Optimising LLM training and serving means raising hardware utilisation and cutting memory and latency without hurting quality.

### Intuition
Training is compute-bound (large matmuls) while decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound, so different techniques apply.

### The math
Training: mixed precision (bf16/fp8), FlashAttention, activation checkpointing (trade 33% compute for memory), data/tensor/pipeline/FSDP parallelism, gradient accumulation, optimised data loading, packing sequences. Serving: KV cache with paged attention, continuous batching, quantisation (int8/int4 weights), speculative decoding (a small draft model proposes k tokens verified in one pass), prefix caching, GQA, tensor parallel inference. Metrics: MFU, tokens/s, time to first token, inter-token latency, cost per million tokens.

### Concrete example
A 70B model quantised to int4 fits on two 80 GB GPUs; with continuous batching and paged attention throughput rises several times versus naive static batching.

### Trade-offs and when to use what
Quantisation trades small quality loss for memory; speculative decoding speeds latency but needs a good draft; larger batches raise throughput but also latency; checkpointing saves memory at compute cost.

### Likely follow-ups
- **What is MFU?** Model FLOPs utilisation: achieved over peak FLOPs.
- **Why is decoding memory-bound?** Each token reads all weights for a few FLOPs.
- **What is continuous batching?** New requests join the batch as others finish.
web-ml-087:
### Definition
Training with noisy human annotators means modelling label noise and annotator reliability so that models learn the true signal rather than the noise.

### Intuition
Annotators disagree through mistakes, ambiguity and bias; treating every label as truth injects noise, while ignoring labels wastes information.

### The math
Approaches: collect multiple labels per item and aggregate (majority vote, Dawid-Skene EM estimating each annotator confusion matrix, weighted voting); use gold questions to score annotators; noise-robust losses (symmetric cross-entropy, bootstrapping, label smoothing); noise-transition matrix correction; confident learning to find mislabelled examples (high loss and confident disagreement); co-teaching, soft labels from annotator distributions; re-annotate ambiguous cases.

### Concrete example
Three annotators label sentiment: labels (pos, pos, neg) give a soft target of (0.67, 0.33); train with cross-entropy to the soft target, and downweight annotators whose agreement with gold items is low.

### Trade-offs and when to use what
More annotators per item improve quality but cost money; spend labels adaptively on disagreeing items. Noise-robust losses help moderate noise but not systematic bias; clean validation data is essential.

### Likely follow-ups
- **What is Dawid-Skene?** EM that jointly estimates labels and annotator confusion matrices.
- **Soft labels versus hard labels?** Soft labels preserve disagreement information.
- **How to detect bad annotators?** Gold items and agreement statistics.
web-ml-088:
### Definition
LLM applications combine a model with prompting, retrieval (RAG), embeddings and vector databases, agents with tools, and retrievers; each part addresses a limitation of the base model.

### Intuition
Prompts steer behaviour, retrieval supplies knowledge, embeddings enable semantic search, and agents let the model act through tools.

### The math
Prompting: instructions, few-shot examples, chain of thought, structured output. Embeddings: dense vectors compared by cosine similarity; vector databases use approximate nearest neighbour indexes (HNSW, IVF-PQ). Retrievers: sparse (BM25), dense bi-encoders, hybrid, rerankers (cross-encoders). Agents: a loop where the model plans, calls tools (search, code, APIs), observes and continues (ReAct), with step limits and guardrails. RAG evaluation: recall@k of the retriever, faithfulness and answer relevance of the generator.

### Concrete example
Support assistant: hybrid retrieval over help articles, rerank top 20 to 5, answer with citations; an agent tool lets it look up order status through an API with permission checks.

### Trade-offs and when to use what
More retrieved context raises recall but dilutes attention and costs tokens; agents add capability but also failure modes (loops, cost, injection); HNSW gives high recall with memory overhead, IVF-PQ compresses at some accuracy loss.

### Likely follow-ups
- **Why a reranker?** Cross-encoders are more accurate than bi-encoders on a short candidate list.
- **How do you evaluate retrieval?** Recall@k and MRR on labelled queries.
- **What limits agents?** Error accumulation, latency and safety.
web-ml-089:
### Definition
Reducing hallucinations needs a measured experiment: define the metric, build an evaluation set, change one mitigation at a time and compare against a baseline.

### Intuition
A hallucination is an unsupported or false claim. You can only reduce what you can measure, so start from a reliable measurement.

### The math
Experiment design: (1) define hallucination (claims unsupported by sources or contradicted by facts); (2) build a test set of prompts including adversarial and unanswerable ones; (3) measure the baseline with claim-level verification (human labels, validated LLM judge, NLI against retrieved sources); (4) candidate interventions: RAG with citations, abstain instructions, lower temperature, self-consistency or verification passes, fine-tuning on grounded data and refusals, decoding constraints; (5) run an A/B comparison with confidence intervals and check side effects (helpfulness, refusal rate, latency).

### Concrete example
Baseline: 18% of answers contain an unsupported claim. With RAG plus a citation requirement: 7%; adding an abstain rule: 5% with refusals up from 2% to 6%; decide by the product trade-off.

### Trade-offs and when to use what
Stronger grounding reduces fabrication but may increase refusals or cost; fully automatic metrics can mislead, so validate them with human audits; separate knowledge gaps from reasoning errors.

### Likely follow-ups
- **How to measure at claim level?** Decompose answers into atomic claims and verify each.
- **Does lower temperature fix it?** Only partly; it reduces randomness not knowledge gaps.
- **What is abstention?** Saying "I don't know" when evidence is missing.
web-ml-090:
### Definition
Retrieval adds external knowledge at inference; fine-tuning stores knowledge and behaviour in the weights. Evaluating an LLM system requires measuring retrieval, generation and end-to-end task quality.

### Intuition
Facts that change or need citations belong in retrieval; skills, style and format belong in fine-tuning.

### The math
Retrieval metrics: recall@k, MRR, nDCG. Generation metrics: faithfulness (claims supported by context), answer relevance, correctness against references, and style compliance. System metrics: latency, cost, refusal behaviour, safety. Evaluation methods: curated golden sets, LLM-as-judge validated against humans, pairwise comparisons, adversarial tests, online A/B tests and user feedback. Track regressions with versioned eval suites.

### Concrete example
Policy chatbot: golden set of 300 questions with expected answers and source pages; measure recall@5 of the retriever (0.92) and faithfulness of answers (0.95), then A/B test against the old FAQ search on resolution rate.

### Trade-offs and when to use what
Retrieval: fresh, auditable, modular; fine-tuning: faster inference, consistent behaviour, but stale and costlier to update. Combine them. Offline evals are fast but may not match user behaviour; online tests are slower but decisive.

### Likely follow-ups
- **When is fine-tuning better?** For stable skills, format and tone.
- **Why separate retrieval and generation metrics?** To locate the failing component.
- **How to catch regressions?** Run the versioned eval suite on every change.
